results.title: DigitalOcean erhöht GPU-Preise: H100 und H200 ab August teurer
highlights:
Die Cloud-Plattform DigitalOcean zieht zum 1. August 2026 die Preise für KI-Grafikprozessoren kräftig an. Der Schritt folgt einem branchenweiten Trend steigender Rechenkosten.

## Preisschub trifft Kunden weltweit

Die neuen Tarife sehen deutliche Aufschläge vor: Die H100-Raten steigen von 3,39 auf 4,41 Euro pro Stunde, die H200-Preise von 3,44 auf 4,47 Euro. Auch für die AMD-Alternative MI300X werden künftig 2,59 Euro fällig. Bestehende Reservierungsverträge bleiben bis zur Verlängerung von den Erhöhungen verschont – Neukunden mit Zwölfmonatsplänen zahlen dagegen sofort die höheren Sätze.

Der Schritt kommt nicht überraschend. Bereits Anfang Januar hatte Amazon Web Services die H200-On-Demand-Preise um 15 Prozent angehoben. Ein Blick auf den Markt zeigt enorme Preisspannen: Über 60 Anbieter verlangen für die H100 zwischen 1,50 und 13 Euro pro Stunde. Besonders volatil zeigte sich der Spot-Markt: Bei AWS fielen die H100-Spot-Preise zwischen Januar 2024 und September 2025 um 88 Prozent.

results.title: What the 2026 GPU Capacity Crunch Did to Rental Prices | AI Compute Marketplace | Compare GPU Cloud & Data Centers | ComputeStacker Insights
highlights:
## What the 2026 GPU capacity crunch did to rental prices

The numbers tell it simply-

| GPU | Mid-2026 rate | The move |
| --- | --- | --- |
| H100 (1-year contract) | ~$2.35/hr | up ~40% since October 2025 |
| H200 | ~$2.80/hr | climbing steadily |
| B200 (Blackwell) | ~$4.90 to $5.64/hr | up 48% in 60 days, roughly doubled |
| B300 | ~$5.29/hr | new premium tier |
| GB300 | ~$5.88/hr | scarcest and priciest |

Older and newer GPUs alike climbed through 2026, the opposite of how hardware usually ages.

Our story starts with the H100, which is just the beginning. The price for 1-year contracts on the H100 rose by 40%, reaching the level of $2.35 per hour in March compared to $1.70 per hour in October. An increase in prices for the outdated processor of two generations back. However, it happens only if there is more demand than supply for the entire stack, not just the top end.

The madness at the top end was even more impressive. The spot rental price on the Blackwell was as high as $4.08 per GPU hour in April, increasing 48% from $2.75 two months earlier, which attracted so much attention that it was mentioned in the Bloomberg Terminal. In July, the price of the B200 tier rose from $3.81 to $5.64. Meanwhile, the price on the Blackwell services increased nearly three times, compared to the previous record of the H100 processor.

Thus, in conclusion, we can say that prices have doubled since January.

## What made it happen: three bottlenecks, a stampede, and everything else going wrong.

But that’s not one bottleneck. That’s three of them happening simultaneously, alongside with the increase in demand.

Packaging. Advanced GPUs need to have the memory attached through CoWoS technology provided by TSMC. And there is no room left whatsoever, none, zero, the calendar is completely booked up at least until mid-2027, which is the absolute maximum limit of accelerators to be physically manufactured. Nothing can be done about it.

Memory. Even more crucial than packaging. Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron have started allocating capacities for the production of memory not for their standard DDR5 and NAND, but for HBM required for AI processors, and HBM3e prices have increased by around 20% in terms of 2026 contracts. AI initiatives are projected to consume up to 40% of global DRAM output. High prices of memory lead to high prices of the entire GPU, regardless of whether the manufacturer had some memory in stock.

Power and cooling. Blackwell GPUs require lots of power and liquid cooling infrastructure, which is not always provided by modern datacenters. Some hyperscalers have Blackwell GPUs already bought, but they are just unable to use them due to insufficient power and memory.

And then came the stampede. Demand surged for inference, not just training. NVIDIA quietly moved its wafer production from H100 to the more profitable Blackwell, which created an even scarcer supply of H100. On top of that, the huge hyperscaler orders that were worth billions of dollars exhausted the rest of NVIDIA’s allocation.

## What really stings: the rent became more difficult, not just expensive

The war was won on price through pricing power. Short-term contracts were put secondary or even pre-emptable, payment was made upfront, and access to capacity required financial commitment. CoreWeave has hiked spot rates more than 20% since December 2025 and started pressuring small customers to enter three-year contracts.

Here is the way the crunch works. It’s not just about hourly prices. The inflexible commitment-oriented approach to cloud GPU rental that used to be the unique feature of the technology is slowly taken away from everyone without any forward commitment contract.

The impact went even to the labs. Outages occurred due to shortages at Anthropic, and OpenAI reduced its product portfolio in an attempt to decrease inference loads. And since they are squeezed, we all are squeezed.

...

At such a close range of prices, from $1.38 per hour to $7.50 per hour, even the availability becomes as uncertain as ever. It’s something that you really do not want to risk.

highlights:
Just this week, cloud infrastructure provider DigitalOcean announced a notable price adjustment plan. Starting August 1st, the platform will increase rental prices for some mainstream GPU instances. Among them, the on-demand prices for the widely favored NVIDIA H100 and H200 instances both rose by about 30%. This wave of cloud compute price hikes has led many teams that were hoping for lower compute costs to start re-evaluating their architecture and financial budgets.

...

According to public adjustment details, starting next month, the on-demand price for NVIDIA H100 instances on the platform will rise from $3.39 per hour to $4.41 per hour. The more powerful H200 instance also rises to $4.47 per hour. Even the AMD MI300X instance sees its on-demand rental price increase to $2.59 per hour.

Not only on-demand instances, but also new or renewed 12-month subscription users will face higher monthly or annual prices. Although users within existing contract periods are temporarily unaffected, research teams running long-term training tasks will face nearly 30% higher compute expenses upon renewal.

In fact, this is not the first time major cloud providers have tested users' tolerance limits. As early as January this year, AWS quietly raised instance prices by 15%. This breaks the traditional pattern in the cloud computing industry where compute unit prices continuously decline with hardware iteration. Most startups can only turn to the GPU rental market for more flexible alternatives.

...

The underlying logic driving this round of price increases primarily stems from tight global upstream supply chains. Although consumer-grade hardware prices have slightly eased, enterprise-grade compute hardware still faces severe supply bottlenecks. With NVIDIA about to mass-produce its Rubin architecture platform, a significant amount of High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) capacity is locked in, making it difficult for memory fabs like Samsung and SK Hynix to alleviate the shortage of enterprise-grade storage chips in the short term.

results.title: GPU Cloud Pricing 2026: What AI Compute Really Costs
highlights:
On January 4, 2026, AWS raised H200 GPU instance prices by 15%. This was the first GPU price increase in roughly two decades. Yet across more than 23,000 Kubernetes clusters in our dataset, the average GPU utilization sits at just 5%. So before that price increase even landed, most teams were already paying for twenty times more GPU capacity than they actually used. The pricing environment just got harder. The utilization problem has not changed.

## Key takeaways

- AWS raised H200 (p5e, p5en) on-demand prices by 15% on January 4, 2026, marking the first GPU price increase in roughly two decades.
- H100 on-demand costs range from $12.29/GPU/hr on AWS (p5.48xlarge) to $13/GPU/hr on Azure. The same GPU type costs up to 6% more depending on which cloud you use.
- Spot and preemptible instances cut costs by 60–91%, but H200 spot availability remains limited across all major clouds.
- Average GPU utilization across Kubernetes clusters is 5%. At that rate, effective GPU cost runs 20x the nominal hourly rate.
- GPU sharing, idle detection, and multi-cloud sourcing reduce effective GPU cost without requiring a change in instance type.

...

## 2026 GPU pricing across clouds: H100, H200, spot vs on-demand

The following table shows on-demand GPU pricing as of mid-2026. Spot savings reflect approximate market discounts and vary by region and availability. For the full dataset and historical trends, see the Cast AI GPU Trends and Cost Report.

| Cloud | Instance | GPUs | GPU Type | On-Demand/hr | Per GPU/hr | Spot Savings |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| AWS | p4d.24xlarge | 8 | A100 40GB | ~$32.77 | ~$4.10 | Up to 80% |
| AWS | p5.48xlarge | 8 | H100 80GB SXM5 | ~$98.32 | ~$12.29 | Up to 70% |
| AWS | p5e.48xlarge | 8 | H200 141GB HBM3e | $39.80 | ~$4.98 | Limited |
| AWS | p5en.48xlarge | 8 | H200 141GB HBM3e | $41.61 | ~$5.20 | Limited |
| GCP | a2-highgpu | 1–8 | A100 | Varies | $2.70–$3.70 | Up to 91% |
| GCP | a3-highgpu-8g | 8 | H100 80GB | ~$80–$90 | $9–$11.50 | Up to 70% |
| Azure | NC A100 v4 | 1–4 | A100 80GB | Varies | $3.50–$4.20 | Up to 80% |
| Azure | ND H100 v5 | 8 | H100 80GB | ~$98 | $11–$13 | Up to 60% |

Note: AWS H200 pricing shown above reflects Capacity Block pricing (1-day or 14-day reservations). On-demand H200 availability on AWS is limited. Capacity Blocks require a commitment upfront, unlike on-demand pay-per-use billing. The H200 per-GPU-hour rate appears lower than H100 because these are Capacity Block commitment rates, not on-demand pricing. Direct on-demand H200 pricing is not generally available on AWS.

...

The GCP H100 (a3-highgpu-8g) runs $80–$90/hr for 8 GPUs ($9–$11.50/GPU/hr on-demand), which is somewhat lower than AWS per-GPU pricing of $12.29/GPU/hr. GCP preemptible instances offer up to 91% savings on A100, making GCP competitive for fault-tolerant training workloads on older GPU hardware. For inference workloads that tolerate interruption, GCP’s A100 preemptible pricing at $2.70–$3.70/GPU/hr represents the lowest effective cost in the market. Azure ND H100 v5 remains the most expensive option at $11–$13/GPU/hr on-demand.

...

Spot and preemptible instances offer 60–91% savings over on-demand for fault-tolerant workloads. In certain AWS regions, H100 Spot now runs approximately $1.95–$2.50/GPU/hr, down as much as 88% from early 2024 peaks in those regions, reflecting growing H100 inventory as data centers scaled capacity. The key requirement is workload checkpointing: training jobs need to resume from the last checkpoint when a spot instance is reclaimed. For inference, stateless containerized services handle preemption well. For guidance on managing GPU shortage and availability risk, automation that spans multiple instance types and fallback options is essential.

results.title: H100 Cloud Pricing 2026: Hourly Rates by Provider
highlights:
NVIDIA H100 cloud rental costs roughly $1.99/hr on RunPod, $2.49/hr on Lambda Labs, and about $1.87/hr on Vast.ai, dropping to ~$1.03/hr on spot (Spheron). Hyperscalers charge far more — up to ~$12/hr on Azure. The most striking fact about H100 pricing in 2026: the same GPU can cost nearly 14x more on one provider than another.

...

## H100 pricing by provider

Rates below are single-GPU H100 hourly prices as of mid-2026. Note that SXM and PCIe variants differ, and spot prices fluctuate constantly.

| Provider | Type | On-demand ($/hr) | Spot ($/hr) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Spheron | Neo-cloud / marketplace | ~$2.50 | ~$1.03 |
| RunPod | Specialized | $1.99 (Community) / $2.89 (Secure) | ~$1.19 |
| Vast.ai | Marketplace (P2P) | ~$1.49–$1.87 | lower, varies |
| Cudo Compute | Neo-cloud | ~$1.80 | — |
| TensorDock | Marketplace | ~$1.99–$2.25 | — |
| Lambda Labs | Specialized | $2.49–$2.99 (SXM), $3.29 (PCIe) | — |
| CoreWeave | Enterprise neo-cloud | ~$6.16 | + spot |
| AWS (p5) | Hyperscaler | ~$6.88 | ~$2.00–$2.50 |
| GCP (a3) | Hyperscaler | ~$3.00–$11.06 | — |
| Azure | Hyperscaler | ~$12.29 | — |

> ⚠️ H100 spot prices can change multiple times per hour. Every figure here is a snapshot — verify live rates before renting.

The takeaway is clear: neo-clouds and marketplaces cluster around $1.50–$3.00/hr, while hyperscalers run 2–5x higher for the identical GPU. If you don’t need enterprise compliance, paying hyperscaler rates for an H100 is usually overpaying.

...

A community thread tracking H100 rates across 25 providers found a 13.8x price difference for the same GPU — from $0.80/hr at the cheapest to over $11/hr at the most expensive. That gap comes down to four factors:

Provider tier. Marketplaces pool spare capacity and compete on price; specialized neo-clouds add reliability at a modest premium; hyperscalers charge most for compliance and integration.

Billing model. Spot/interruptible rates undercut on-demand by 50–80%. The Spheron spot floor of ~$1.03/hr versus its $2.50/hr on-demand shows the size of that discount.

GPU variant. The H100 SXM (higher bandwidth, NVLink) and H100 PCIe are priced differently — and how a provider publishes the price matters too. Hyperscalers often quote a full VM (compute, memory, storage bundled), which inflates the headline number versus a “naked GPU” rate.

Region and availability. Capacity-constrained regions cost more, and prices shift as supply changes.

...

H100 rental has become dramatically cheaper since its 2023 launch. Early adopters paid rates like $7–11/hr on hyperscalers; by 2026 specialist clouds routinely offer the same GPU under $3/hr. The arrival of the B200 (Blackwell) is pushing H100 prices down further as data centers upgrade and demand shifts to newer silicon. If you’re renting H100s, this trend works in your favor — but it also means any quoted price ages quickly.

results.title: A GPU-Hour Isn't a Commodity If You Need Four of Them
highlights:
I recently surveyed 1 GPU rental prices on Vast.ai, the compute rental marketplace. An H200 rented for about $3.93 per GPU-hour. Without knowing anything else, it looks pretty straightforward. You pick the chip, you multiply the hourly rate by the number of GPUs you need and the number of hours you need, and you get an invoice.

But if you want four identical H200s in the same machine, half the qualifying supply disappears, and the remaining supply costs 4% more. If you want eight, you’re out of luck: there’s nothing in the sample at any price. The rental rate and the price of usable compute are different numbers.

...

The headlines say that an H100 costs one amount, and a B200 a different amount.

...

An interesting result of this analysis is that larger clusters don’t necessarily cost more. Supply of large clusters thins as the requested cluster grows, usually with no matching move in the quoted price. H200 shows this most cleanly. Going from one GPU to two left 92% of listed physical inventory eligible at essentially the same price. Going to four cut eligible inventory to 50% while the price measure rose 4%, from $3.93 to $4.08 per GPU-hour. At eight GPUs, nothing qualified.

Supply of H100 and B200 were thinner still. Qualifying H100 supply supported a two-GPU request but not a four-GPU one. The B200 sample held two physical machines, both topping out at two GPUs, so four- and eight-GPU availability was zero. A100 behaved like you would expect: price increased as supply declined. Eight-GPU machines existed, and the price measure climbed from $0.60 per GPU-hour at the one-GPU baseline to $1.29, a contiguity premium of 114%. L40S cut both ways. Only 35% of its listed inventory sat in machines big enough for an eight-GPU request, but the one machine that qualified was cheap. This is a thin cross-sectional order book, not a smooth supply curve.

results.title: GPU Shortage Returns: Microsoft Prioritizes OpenAI, AI Startups Face 32% Rent Hike and Months-Long Queues | Bit.Fan
highlights:
Cloud giants like Microsoft and Amazon are funneling NVIDIA GPU capacity to internal teams and top clients OpenAI/Anthropic, squeezing smaller AI startups with 32% price hikes, waitlists through year-end, and multi-million-dollar contract minimums. VCs are pooling resources; one startup is buying hardware outright.

40,000 GPUs online, 400,000 waiting in line. According to The Information, Lightning AI CEO Will Falcon put a precise number on it: the supply-demand ratio for AI compute in 2026 is 1 to 10. His platform has roughly 40 customers queuing, and rental prices have surged over 25% in the past six months.

### From $2.80 to $3.70: Renewal Shock

Image-generation startup Krea (83 million in funding from Andreessen Horowitz and Bain Capital Ventures) rented hundreds of NVIDIA Blackwell chips six months ago at $2.80 per card per hour on a six-month contract. When renewal time came, multiple cloud providers simply stopped answering calls. The final price was $3.70 — a 32% spike — and the contract term was stretched to one year. CEO Victor Perez said some vendors demanded a three-year commitment before even discussing terms; others never replied.

The Ornn Compute Price Index shows Blackwell hourly rates have hit $4.08, up 48% in two months. One-year H100 leases jumped from $1.70 in October 2025 to $2.35 in March 2026, a near-40% increase.

...

Microsoft has instituted a tiered GPU access system. The top 1,000 customers (Tier 1) get first dibs on compute. Smaller clients wanting Blackwell must commit to at least 1,000 chips for at least one year, with contracts starting at tens of millions of dollars. Pay-as-you-go customers risk losing access if GPUs sit idle for a few hours; startups on the Microsoft for Startups free credit plan are warned that underutilization will result in revocation of GPU permissions. Azure sales management recently told staff that GPU wait times for cloud customers are expected to persist until the end of 2026. The bulk of compute now goes to OpenAI, Anthropic, and other big accounts, leaving smaller AI startups in a perpetual queue.

results.title: Computable startet Auktionsplattform für GPU-Leistung mit flexiblen Mietmodellen
highlights:
Das Startup Computable bietet erstmals eine Auktionsplattform für GPU-Leistung an. Nutzer können Rechenzeit auf NVIDIA-H100-Chips wochenweise ersteigern, mit dynamischer Vergabe und ohne langfristige Verträge.

Das Berliner Startup Computable hat eine Online-Plattform vorgestellt, auf der Unternehmen und Einzelpersonen Rechenleistung von Grafikprozessoren (GPUs) flexibel und zeitlich begrenzt mieten können. Anders als viele klassische Cloud-Angebote mit festen Preisen und längerfristigen Verträgen setzt Computable auf wöchentliche Auktionen. Seit Juli 2026 ist die Plattform öffentlich zugänglich. Sie richtet sich an Nutzerinnen und Nutzer mit kurzfristigem Bedarf an leistungsfähigen KI-Chips.

...

Interessierte wählen in einer Kalenderansicht die benötigten Wochen aus und geben ein Gebot für den gewünschten Zeitraum ab. Den Zuschlag erhält nicht ausschließlich das höchste Gebot: Ein dynamischer Prioritäts-Score soll auch kleineren Projekten mit begrenztem Budget Zugang erlauben. Nach Unternehmensangaben orientiert sich das Modell an Prinzipien aus dem Energiemarkt. Es soll Preistransparenz und Flexibilität unterstützen.

Zum Start stehen NVIDIA-H100-Grafikprozessoren bereit. Die Auktionen umfassen Zeiträume von August 2026 bis Januar 2027. Das Startgebot lag bei 2,42 US-Dollar pro GPU-Stunde, erste Gebote stiegen auf etwa 2,62 US-Dollar. Bei einer einzelnen GPU und durchgehender Nutzung über eine volle Woche, also 168 Stunden, ergibt dieser Stundensatz rechnerisch 440,16 US-Dollar. Ein Gesamtpreis von etwas mehr als 300 US-Dollar für dieselbe Nutzungsdauer entspräche dagegen einem effektiven Preis von rund 1,79 US-Dollar pro Stunde. Der Wochenbetrag hängt also davon ab, ob die GPU tatsächlich rund um die Uhr genutzt wird und welcher Preis für die gebuchte Kapazität gilt.

...

Die Preise für H100-Kapazität unterscheiden sich je nach Anbieter und Verfügbarkeitsmodell. Vergleichsangebote für eine H100 SXM lagen im Oktober 2026 etwa bei 1,73 US-Dollar pro Stunde bei Vast.ai, 2,69 US-Dollar im Community-Modell von RunPod und 3,99 US-Dollar in dessen Secure Cloud. Eine H100-Mietpreisübersicht von Spheron führte zudem On-Demand-Angebote mit unterschiedlichen Serverkonfigurationen auf: darunter 2,21 US-Dollar pro Stunde für einen einzelnen H100-PCIe-Spot-Server und 2,75 US-Dollar je GPU-Stunde in einem Acht-GPU-H100-NVL-System. Die Unterschiede spiegeln neben dem Preis auch Kapazität und Host-Vertrauen wider; hinzu kommen die jeweiligen Leistungszusagen.

Weitere Marktvergleiche ordneten Marketplace- und Spot-Angebote ungefähr zwischen 1,70 und 2,00 US-Dollar pro GPU-Stunde ein. Dedizierte Cloud-Kapazität lag zwischen etwa 2,00 und 3,00 US-Dollar; Jahresverträge wurden mit rund 2,35 bis 2,50 US-Dollar angegeben. Für On-Demand-H100-Leistung reichte die Spanne je nach Anbieter und Region im Oktober 2026 von ungefähr 2 bis 12 US-Dollar pro Stunde. Auch Bündelgröße und Abrechnungsmodell wirkten sich auf den Preis aus. Spheron nannte für den 23. Oktober 2026 einen On-Demand-Preis von 2,64 US-Dollar je Stunde bei einem Abrechnungsminimum von 20 Minuten. Wegen der unterschiedlichen GPU-Ausführungen und Vertragsbedingungen sind diese Preise keine unmittelbaren Eins-zu-eins-Vergleiche.

results.title: The GPU Market Has Two Prices | GPUaaS.com
highlights:
A hyperscaler quotes $10.60 an hour for an H200. A wholesale buyer gets the same chip for $3.79 to $4.54. Neither number is fake. Both are real prices for the same GPU, quoted to two different buyers in two different markets.

...

Key takeaways

- H100 retail held steady at $25,000 to $40,000 from mid-2024 into early 2026, while the secondary market swung from $50,000 during 2024's scarcity peak down to $21,000-$34,000 refurbished as of Q2 2026
- Hyperscaler H200 on-demand runs around $10.60/hr versus $3.79 to $4.54/hr wholesale for the same silicon
- A100 cloud rental rates range $1.29 to $3.43/hr depending on provider, nearly a 3x spread for the same chip
- The retail price is quoted to whoever asks casually. The clearing price moves with real-time supply and demand among buyers actually transacting
- Q2 2026 secondary supply is loosening further as B200 deployments accelerate, with continued softening expected on H100 and A100 inventory specifically

...

The same split shows up in rental rates, not just purchase price. Hyperscaler on-demand carries a premium built for buyers who need the full managed stack, global region coverage, compliance certification, native tooling. Specialized providers price the same H200 silicon closer to what the hardware costs to run, without the bundle. Both numbers are legitimate. They're pricing different things wrapped around the same chip.

...

The A100 tells the same story from a different angle. Cloud rental rates for A100 now range $1.29 to $3.43 an hour depending on provider, a spread wide enough that the cheapest and most expensive quotes for the same chip differ by nearly 3x. Purchase prices for used A100s are projected to fall another 10 to 15% through the rest of 2026 as more enterprises move to Blackwell-generation hardware. Every generation this happens to. The retail number for the current chip stays put while the secondary and rental markets for it, and for whatever it's replacing, move constantly underneath.

...

For H200, hyperscaler on-demand runs around $10.60 an hour versus $3.79 to $4.54 an hour wholesale for the same silicon. For A100 rentals, rates range $1.29 to $3.43 an hour depending on provider, nearly a 3x spread. These gaps vary by chip generation and current market conditions.
